1.synthesis:
Agni is asked to carry. Everything given into the fire rises through him, and the gods arrive through him — that is the premise the hymn opens on, and the reason the collection begins here rather than with sky or storm. Agni is the god who is actually present, burning on the hearth, and so he is where contact begins.

*Agnim īḷe* — I praise Agni. The first verse gives him four titles, and each names work rather than glory. *Purohitam*, the one placed in front, who stands at the head of the rite. *Ṛtvijam*, the one who officiates when the season calls for it. *Hotāram*, the one who offers — and, in the older sense, the one who calls the gods by name. *Ratnadhātama*, the greatest holder of what is precious. The god is being described entirely through what he does for those who approach him.

The second verse makes a claim about time that is easy to read past. Agni is *īḍya* — worthy of praise — by the *pūrve ṛṣayaḥ*, the seers of long ago, and equally by the *nūtana*, those alive now. The same fire, the same address, across a distance nobody can measure. And the verse ends with the undertaking: *sa devāṁ eha vakṣati*, he shall convey the gods here. Anyone who recites the line steps into precisely what the line describes.

The third and fourth verses say what comes of it. Through Agni a person reaches *rayi* — wealth, but wealth as sustenance rather than hoard — and *poṣa*, nourishment that increases *dive-dive*, day upon day, along with *yaśas*, good standing, and strength in sons. Then the mechanism behind it: the *yajña* that Agni surrounds *viśvataḥ*, on every side, arrives among the gods. The word used for that offering is *adhvara* — the rite that suffers no injury, that nothing breaks into. Being encircled by fire is what keeps it whole.

The fifth verse turns from what Agni does to what he is: *hotā* again, and *kavikratu* — one in whom insight and effective action are the same faculty — and *satya*, true, and of the most brilliant renown. It closes *devo devebhir ā gamat*: the god comes, bringing the gods. The promise made in the second verse is fulfilled here, three verses later, and the hymn does not point this out.

The sixth verse states a law of the exchange. *Yad aṅga dāśuṣe tvaṃ agne bhadraṃ kariṣyasi, tavet tat satyam* — whatever good you do for the one who gives, that is your own truth. The generosity is not the worshipper's to claim; it belongs to Agni, and it returns. He is addressed here as *Aṅgiras*, a seer's name given to fire.

The seventh and eighth verses describe the approach itself, and they belong together. *Upa tvā... emasi* — we come near to you, *dive-dive*, day upon day, at the turning of dusk and dawn, *dhiyā*, with the mind engaged, *namo bharantaḥ*, bearing homage. And the one approached is: ruler of the rites, *gopām ṛtasya* — herdsman of ṛta, the one who keeps the order of things — shining, and *vardhamānaṃ sve dame*, growing in his own house. The fire that grows in your home is the same fire that guards the order of the world.

Then the ninth verse sets all of it down. After eight verses of office and function, of titles and powers, it asks for none of them: *sa naḥ piteva sūnave... sūpāyano bhava* — be easy to approach, as a father is to a son; stay near us, *svastaye*, for our wellbeing. The oldest prayer that survives in the tradition ends by asking the fire that mediates everything to be, before anything else, approachable.
1.disagreements:
The tradition and the translators divide over *hotṛ*, the office named in verses 1 and 5. Sāyaṇa gives two derivations without choosing between them: from *hu*, to pour an offering, or from *hve*, to call — the one who sends the oblation up, or the one who summons the gods down. He identifies the hotā with the ṛtvij, citing the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. Wilson follows the pouring sense throughout ("who presents the oblation"); Griffith leaves *hotar* untranslated in verse 1 and renders it "sapient-minded Priest" in verse 5.

On verse 6, Wilson has Agni's good "revert to you, Aṅgiras" — a circuit in which what is given comes back. Griffith reads a statement of reliability instead: "That, Angiras, is indeed thy truth." Sāyaṇa explains the vocative by deriving Aṅgiras from *aṅgāra*, a live coal, citing the Nirukta and the Brāhmaṇa tradition that the coals became the Aṅgirasas — which is why a fire can be addressed by a seer's name.

Verse 7's *doṣāvastar* splits them: Wilson takes it as dusk and dawn together, describing when the worshippers come; Griffith makes it an epithet of Agni, "dispeller of the night." Sāyaṇa reads verse 4's "on every side" concretely — the ritual fires standing at the four cardinal points of the enclosure — and glosses *adhvara* as the sacrifice free from injury or interruption.

1.practice:
This is the first hymn a student of the Ṛgveda receives, and the fire it addresses is not a historical object. Agni is still the witness before whom the saṃskāras are performed — the fire circled at a wedding, kindled at the upanayana, lit at the last rite. Whatever else has changed, the addressee has not.

The sūkta also describes its own use. Verse 7 has the worshippers coming *dive-dive*, day upon day, at the turn of dusk and dawn, bearing homage *dhiyā* — with thought, not only with words. That is the sandhyā rhythm, stated in the text itself: not an occasional approach but a daily one, at the junctures, with attention. The hymn is not asking to be read once.

What it offers for reflection is the shape of the ninth verse. The relationship it finally asks for is not the awe due to power, but the ease a son has with his father — *sūpāyano bhava*, be easy of approach. Everything preceding establishes Agni's authority; the last line asks him to set it aside. That order is deliberate, and it is the hymn's teaching.
1.title: Fire Given Every Title, Then Asked to Be a Father

2.synthesis:
The soma has been pressed and stands ready. What follows is not praise so much as hospitality — the drinkers are called in a fixed order, three verses each, and the order is itself the meaning. Wind first, then strength, and last the two who hold the world in its courses.

*Vāyav ā yāhi darśata* — Vāyu, come, you who are worth the sight. The somas are *araṃkṛtāḥ*, made ready, and the god is asked to do two things: drink, and hear. *Śrudhī havam* — listen to the call. Both halves matter, because the hymn is about to record that the call is answered.

The second verse names who is doing the calling. The *jaritāraḥ*, the singers, praise Vāyu with *ukthas* — recited verses, not chanted ones — and they are *sutasomāḥ*, having pressed the soma, and *aharvidaḥ*, knowers of the days. That last word is quiet but exact: these are people who know which day is the right day. The rite has a calendar, and they hold it.

Then the third verse turns the direction around. Vāyu's *dhenā* — his speech, his stream — goes out *dāśuṣe*, toward the one who gave, and it is *urūcī*, wide-reaching, and it comes *somapītaye*, for the drinking. The god is not merely summoned; something moves back down the line toward the worshipper.

The three Indra-and-Vāyu verses quicken. The pressed drops are set out, and the two are asked to come *upa prayobhiḥ*, with their pleasures — and then the hymn says something startling: *indavo vām uśanti hi*, the drops themselves desire you. The wanting is not only on the human side. The fifth verse calls the pair *vājinīvasū*, rich in the substance of strength, and asks them to come *dravat*, running. The sixth asks them to the *niṣkṛtam*, the appointed place — the spot prepared for the meeting — *makṣu*, quickly, and *itthā dhiyā*, thus with the mind's attention. Speed and attention together: the hurry is not carelessness.

The last three verses change register entirely. *Mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣaṃ varuṇaṃ ca riśādasam* — I call Mitra, whose *dakṣa*, whose effective power, is pure, and Varuṇa who destroys hostility. They are asked to perfect a *dhī* that is *ghṛtācī*, ghee-bearing: the thought itself is described as carrying an offering, as if the mind were a ladle.

The eighth verse is the hymn's centre of gravity, and it hammers one word. *Ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā* — by ṛta, O Mitra and Varuṇa, growers of ṛta, touchers of ṛta. Three of the verse's words are built on the same root, and by it the two have attained *kratuṃ bṛhantam*, vast effective power. Ṛta is at once the truth of things, the working of the waters, and the sacrifice: to say the pair grow by it, increase it, and are in contact with it is to say they are what keeps the world running true.

The ninth closes by asking for something modest after all that height. The two are *kavī*, seers, *tuvijātā*, strong-born, *urukṣayā*, wide-dwelling — and what they are asked to bestow is *dakṣam apasam*, skill that works. Not visions. Competence.
2.practice:
These are the deities of the daily offering, and the order the hymn calls them in is the order of a rite still performed: the wind that carries, the strength that arrives, and last the pair who hold things in their courses.

Mitra and Varuṇa arrive here as a pair, and that is how they nearly always arrive. Across the whole Ṛgveda thirty-six sūktas are ascribed to *mitrāvaruṇau* — the two named as a single dual compound — and exactly one, [[3.59]], is addressed to Mitra by himself. Out of 1,028 hymns, Mitra stands alone once. Whatever these two are, the tradition treats them as one thing with two faces, which is why they can be asked in a single breath to perfect the thought and grant working skill.

The division between those faces is the one every Hindu who performs sandhyāvandana keeps. Mitra presides over the day and Varuṇa over the night, and *sandhyā* is exactly the observance of the junctures where one hands over to the other — the arghya offered as the day begins and again as it closes. The rite is built on the same division this hymn names. And the single Mitra sūkta supplies one of sandhyā's own verses: *mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛto 'vo devasya sānasi*, the sustaining favour of Mitra who upholds the peoples ([[3.59]].6).

*Ṛta* is what to carry away. It is the word for the order that turns the seasons, moves the waters, and makes a promise hold — and the same word for the sacrifice. To act in accordance with ṛta and to perform the rite correctly are not two different things in this vocabulary. Mitra and Varuṇa are asked here not for favour but for that order to be maintained, and for *dakṣam apasam*, skill that actually works.

One caution about the word, because a near neighbour of it is in every pūjā. *Ṛta* is not *ṛtu*. *Ṛtu* is the season — the word named in the saṅkalpa when the time of the rite is declared, *ṛtau, māse, pakṣe*. *Ṛta* is the order itself. They are separate words that share the root √ṛ, to move or go, and the shared idea is regular recurrent motion: a season is what comes round again on time, and ṛta is the order by which anything comes round at all. The overlap is genuine — across the Ṛgveda *ṛta* appears in some 76 analysed forms and *ṛtu* in 20, and the glosses bleed into each other, "order" sitting inside ṛtu and "timely" inside ṛta.

The join between them is a word from the first hymn. *Ṛtvij*, the officiating priest — the title given to Agni in [[1.1]].1 — is *ṛtu* + √yaj, one who sacrifices at the proper season. The priest is named for the season, not for the truth. Doing the thing at its right time is itself how the order is kept.
2.disagreements:
*Ṛta* is where the readings part, and it is the most consequential divergence in the hymn. Wilson keeps the concrete range — Mitra and Varuṇa as "augmenters of water, dispensers of water" who connect the rite to its true reward — because Sāyaṇa allows the word to carry water and sacrifice alongside truth. Griffith goes to the abstraction: "through Law, lovers and cherishers of Law." One pair makes the rains work; the other upholds a principle.

Verse 3 divides the same way. Wilson's Vāyu answers with approving speech, and Sāyaṇa supplies the god's words outright — *I will drink the libation*. Griffith has "thy penetrating stream goes forth unto the worshipper," which makes it wind rather than reply.

Sāyaṇa identifies Mitra with the sun and Varuṇa with the regent of the waters, both among the twelve Ādityas, with Mitra presiding over the day and Varuṇa over the night.
2.title: The Cup Goes Round Until Ṛta Is Named

3.synthesis:
Twelve verses, four guests, three verses each. The Aśvins come first — twin horsemen, quick-handed, asked to take the offering with outstretched hands and to hear the praise without turning away. Indra follows, drawn by tawny horses, and the soma set out for him has been pressed and purified by the priests' own fingers; the hymn keeps that detail because it matters that the work was done by hand. Then the All-Gods together, asked to come as swiftly as the sun's rays come to the day.

Then Sarasvatī, and the hymn opens onto something wider than the rite. She is called purifier, the one who answers worship with abundance, the inspirer of those who delight in truth and the guide of the well-minded. And in the final verse she is both at once: she makes a great river visible, and she lights up every understanding. The hymn does not choose between the two and does not treat one as a figure for the other. A river running through the land and the clarity that arrives in a mind are named as the same power.

That refusal to resolve is the hymn's most valuable move. Sarasvatī is the earliest place in the collection where something is held as fully outward and fully inward at once — a presence you could walk to, and a faculty you could recognise in yourself.
3.practice:
Sarasvatī's two aspects are why this hymn still matters outside a study. She is invoked here as a river you could stand beside and as the power that clarifies thought, and the text holds both without apology. The tradition that later made her the patron of speech, learning, and music is already present in these three verses — *the inspirer of those who delight in truth, the guide of the well-minded*.

The hymn is also a reminder that the Aśvins were approached as healers. Where illness or recovery is the concern, this is the address the tradition preserved: twin riders, quick to arrive, called to the offering with their hands already outstretched.
3.disagreements:
Sarasvatī's doubling is where the translators separate. Wilson keeps both aspects as genuinely two — she manifests a mighty river, and in her own form enlightens all understandings. Sāyaṇa states the position directly, citing the Nirukta that Sarasvatī is twofold, an embodied deity and a river, and that the hymns speak of her in both ways. Griffith compresses to "the mighty flood — she with her light illuminates, She brightens every pious thought," which reads the river as metaphor for the mind.

Verse 9 turns on a single epithet. Wilson's All-Gods are "exempt from decay, omniscient, devoid of malice"; Griffith's are "changing shape like serpents, fearless, void of guile." Sāyaṇa offers two readings of the word himself — those whose knowledge extends everywhere, or a name from the legend in which the gods called to Agni in the water, *ehi, mā yāsiḥ*, come, do not go.

On the Aśvins, Sāyaṇa records the tradition that they are the physicians of the gods, and takes their epithet *rudravartani* as those who travel at the head of the warriors, deriving *rudra* from the root for weeping — those who make their enemies weep.
3.title: Four Guests Called, and a River That Is Also a Mind
